q-85150.name: Question 1
q-85150.problem: A writer is editing the first draft of a book. On average, there have been $4$ typos per page. What is the probability of finding $2$ typos on the next page? Round your answer to $3$ decimal places. You may assume that typos occur independently and at a constant average rate.
q-85150.worked_solution:
A Poisson random variable $X$ with rate $\lambda $ has the following probability mass function:

$$
f(x)=\frac{{\lambda }^{x}{e}^{-\lambda }}{x!}
$$

Let $X$ be the number of typos on a page of the book. Since the average rate is $4$ typos per page, and events occur independently and at a constant average rate, the number of typos can be modeled as a Poisson random variable with rate $\lambda =4,$ and we can write $X∼\text{Po}(4).$

So, $X$ has the following probability mass function:

$$
f(x)=\frac{{4}^{x}{e}^{-4}}{x!}
$$

Therefore, the probability of finding $2$ typos on the next page is

$$
\begin{aligned}P(X=2) & =f(2) \\  & =\frac{{4}^{2}{e}^{-4}}{2!} \\  & ≈0.147\end{aligned}
$$

rounded to $3$ decimal places.

a
 0.173
b
 0.115
c
 0.147
d
 0.500
e
 0.238
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

A Poisson random variable X with rate λ has the following probability mass function:

f(x)=λxe−λx!

Let X be the number of typos on a page of the book. Since the average rate is 4 typos per page, and events occur independently and at a constant average rate, the number of typos can be modeled as a Poisson random variable with rate λ=4, and we can write X∼Po(4).

q-85394.name: Question 2
q-85394.problem: A telephone exchange receives an average of $7$ calls every $5$ minutes. What is the probability that the exchange will receive at least $5$ calls in the next $5$ minutes? Round your answer to $3$ decimal places. You may assume that calls occur independently and at a constant average rate.
q-85394.worked_solution:
A Poisson random variable $X$ with rate $\lambda $ has the following probability mass function:

$$
f(x)=\frac{{\lambda }^{x}{e}^{-\lambda }}{x!}
$$

Let $X$ be the number of calls received in the telephone exchange. Since the average rate is $7$ calls every $5$ minutes, and events occur independently and at a constant average rate, the number of calls can be modeled as a Poisson random variable with rate $\lambda =7,$ and we can write $X∼\text{Po}(7).$ 

So, $X$ has the following probability mass function:

$$
f(x)=\frac{{7}^{x}{e}^{-7}}{x!}
$$

To compute $P(X\ge 5),$ we will use the complement:

$$
P(X\ge 5)=1-P(X<5)
$$

Computing the probability of the complement, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}P(X<5) & =P(X\in \{0,1,2,3,4\}) \\  & =f(0)+f(1)+f(2)+f(3)+f(4) \\  & =\frac{{7}^{0}{e}^{-7}}{0!}+\frac{{7}^{1}{e}^{-7}}{1!}+\frac{{7}^{2}{e}^{-7}}{2!}+\frac{{7}^{3}{e}^{-7}}{3!}+\frac{{7}^{4}{e}^{-7}}{4!} \\  & ≈0.173\end{aligned}
$$

rounded to $3$ decimal places.

Therefore, the probability of receiving at least $5$ calls in the next $5$ minutes is

$$
\begin{aligned}P(X\ge 5) & =1-P(X<5) \\  & ≈1-0.173 \\  & =0.827\end{aligned}
$$

rounded to $3$ decimal places.

q-131276.name: Question 4
q-131276.problem: The mean number of bacteria per milliliter of a liquid is $6.$ What is the probability that there will be no more than $3$ bacteria in one milliliter of the liquid? Round your answer to $3$ decimal places. You may assume that bacteria appear independently and at a constant average rate.
q-131276.worked_solution:
A Poisson random variable $X$ with rate $\lambda $ has the following probability mass function:

$$
f(x)=\frac{{\lambda }^{x}{e}^{-\lambda }}{x!}
$$

Let $X$ be the number of bacteria in one milliliter of the liquid. Since the average rate is $6$ bacteria per milliliter, and events occur independently and at a constant average rate, the number of bacteria can be modeled as a Poisson random variable with rate $\lambda =6,$ and we can write $X∼\text{Po}(6).$

So, $X$ has the following probability mass function:

$$
f(x)=\frac{{6}^{x}{e}^{-6}}{x!}
$$

Therefore, the probability that at most $3$ bacteria will be found in one milliliter of the liquid is

$$
\begin{aligned}P(X\le 3) & =P(X\in \{0,1,2,3\}) \\  & =f(0)+f(1)+f(2)+f(3) \\  & =\frac{{6}^{0}{e}^{-6}}{0!}+\frac{{6}^{1}{e}^{-6}}{1!}+\frac{{6}^{2}{e}^{-6}}{2!}+\frac{{6}^{3}{e}^{-6}}{3!} \\  & ≈0.151\end{aligned}
$$

rounded to $3$ decimal places.

q-131281.problem: Previous results indicate that, on average, for each batch of transistors, $1$ is defective. q-131281.worked_solution:
A Poisson random variable $X$ with rate $\lambda $ has the following probability mass function:

$$
f(x)=\frac{{\lambda }^{x}{e}^{-\lambda }}{x!}
$$

Let $X$ be the number of defective transistors in a batch of transistors. Since the average rate is $1$ defective transistors per batch, and events occur independently and at a constant average rate, the number of defective transistors can be modeled as a Poisson random variable with rate $\lambda =1,$ and we can write $X∼\text{Po}(1).$

So, $X$ has the following probability mass function:

$$
f(x)=\frac{{1}^{x}{e}^{-1}}{x!}
$$

Therefore, the probability that in the next batch of transistors, there will be less than $4$ defective transistors is

$$
\begin{aligned}P(X<4) & =P(X\in \{0,1,2,3\}) \\  & =f(0)+f(1)+f(2)+f(3) \\  & =\frac{{1}^{0}{e}^{-1}}{0!}+\frac{{1}^{1}{e}^{-1}}{1!}+\frac{{1}^{2}{e}^{-1}}{2!}+\frac{{1}^{3}{e}^{-1}}{3!} \\  & ≈0.981\end{aligned}
$$

rounded to $3$ decimal places.

q-131281.html:
Question 5
?

Previous results indicate that, on average, for each batch of transistors, 1 is defective. What is the probability that in the next batch of transistors, there will be less than 4 defective transistors? Round your answer to 3 decimal places. You may assume that defective transistors occur independently and at a constant average rate.

a
0.907
b
0.881
c
0.981
d
0.904
e
0.890
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

A Poisson random variable X with rate λ has the following probability mass function: f(x)=λxe−λx!

Let X be the number of defective transistors in a batch of transistors. Since the average rate is 1 defective transistors per batch, and events occur independently and at a constant average rate, the number of defective transistors can be modeled as a Poisson random variable with rate λ=1, and we can write X∼Po(1).

So, X has the following probability mass function: f(x)=1xe−1x!

Therefore, the probability that in the next batch of transistors, there will be less than 4 defective transistors is P(X<4)=P(X∈{0,1,2,3})=f(0)+f(1)+f(2)+f(3)=10e−10!+11e−11!+12e−12!+13e−13!≈0.981 rounded to 3 decimal places.
